note: The worked example for the schema. US cuts in this atlas are IMPS primals, which is the easy case for bounds (they are defined by named ribs and joints) and the hard case for sources: IMPS Series 100 is unreachable live -- 403 at ams.usda.gov, login at meattrack.com -- but a copy of the November 2014 PDF was recovered from an earlier pass's cache and its text is reproduced verbatim in imps-items.md, which is what the boundary quotes cite. Muscle lists lean on CFIA, whose Canadian primals share the American cutting lines, and on the Calkins & Sullivan table reproduced in calkins-table.md. Quotes here are strictly the text a fetch returned inside quotation marks; where a source numbers its clauses, the number is a `locator` on the source rather than part of the quote. WebFetch paraphrases and merges adjacent passages unless asked for verbatim text, so anything assembled around a quoted fragment is a fabrication waiting to be trusted.

cuts.dispute: IMPS Series 100 is quoted directly now: a copy of the November 2014 PDF was recovered and its text is reproduced in imps-items.md. This is the pairing most often published inverted — BBQ writing routinely swaps flat and point. TAMU (IMPS/English naming), UNL (Latin) and IMAIOS (NAV) agree: flat = deep pectoral = pectoralis profundus = pectoralis ascendens; point = superficial pectoral. UNL puts the word 'Deckle' on both entries, so do not disambiguate from UNL alone.

No beef source enumerates the foreshank's muscles, for the same reason as the hind shank: none of it is sold as a named muscle, it is shin and osso buco on the bone. The list is bovine forelimb anatomy, not a butchery claim, and is graded inferred accordingly. Bounds: IMPS 117 is a straight cut exposing a cross-section of the humerus, parted from the brisket along the natural seam — from the atlas's own IMPS-based region text, not quotable.
